optArrow is an open-source mathematical optimisation platform. Think of it as a system that takes a real-world problem (such as minimising cost, maximising efficiency, or finding the best design for a mechanical part), translates it into mathematical equations, and then uses powerful solvers to find the best possible answer.

For example, an engineer might ask: "What is the minimum-cost beam design that can support a 500N load without exceeding stress limits?" optArrow would take this question, formulate it as a mathematical optimisation problem, send it to a solver, and return the optimal design.
The platform is built in layers, like a sandwich. Each layer has a specific job. Here is every layer, explained simply:
How users interact with optArrow. They can either use a web page in their browser, or type commands in a terminal (like VS Code). Both send requests to the server.

The "front door" of the server. Every request from every client comes here first. FastAPI is a modern Python web framework that handles HTTP requests, validates inputs, and routes work to the right engine. Think of it as a receptionist.

One of two "brains" for building optimisation models. Pyomo is a Python library that lets you write optimisation problems as Python code. Arrow Flight RPC is a high-speed data transfer protocol (like a superhighway for data) that connects FastAPI to Pyomo.
The second "brain." JuMP is similar to Pyomo but written in Julia (a language designed for high-performance scientific computing). It connects to FastAPI via a simple TCP socket.

The actual "number crunchers." Once Pyomo or JuMP formulates the mathematical problem, it hands it to one of these solvers. Each solver is like a specialist: HiGHS is free and fast for linear problems; MOSEK handles conic/SOCP; Gurobi is commercial-grade; GLPK is a classic open-source choice; Hypatia handles exotic cone types.

Key technical detail: The codebase is 66% Python, 16% Julia, 13% MATLAB, and the rest is Shell scripts and Dockerfiles. The full source code lives at github.com/optArrow/optArrow and the documentation site is at optarrow.github.io/optArrow/.
2. What is RAG and Why Do We Need It?
Right now, optArrow is powerful but "silent." It can solve optimisation problems if you give it perfectly formatted input, but it cannot answer questions like:
"Which solver should I use for a second-order cone problem?"
"Show me how to define constraints in Pyomo for a beam design."
"What does the JuMP engine's error code 42 mean?"
"Find me similar past projects with these constraints."
Users currently have to dig through documentation, source code, and solver manuals manually. This is slow, error-prone, and creates a steep learning curve for new team members.

RAG is a technique that makes an AI assistant (like ChatGPT or Claude) smarter by giving it access to your own documents. Instead of the AI making up answers from its general training, RAG works in three steps:
Step 1 (Retrieve): Search your documents (code, PDFs, manuals) to find the most relevant passages.
Step 2 (Augment): Attach those passages to the AI's prompt so it has real context.
Step 3 (Generate): The AI writes an answer based only on those real documents, with citations.

The result is an AI copilot that can answer questions about optArrow accurately, cite its sources, and even trigger optimisation runs on your behalf. It never hallucinates because it only answers from your actual documents.
What We Are Building: The Spindle Copilot Architecture

The RAG architecture we are implementing is based on a multi-agent copilot design. It is not just a simple question-answer bot. It has multiple specialised AI agents that each handle different types of tasks:
Receives user queries, plans a strategy, delegates to sub-agents, and compiles the final answer with citations.
"Solve kinematics for these customer requirements" → plans research + iteration + summary steps
Answers knowledge questions by searching the vector database, SQL store, and docs site.
"What are the material numbers for spindle bearings?" or "How does the Pyomo engine handle SOCP?"
Runs optimisation loops using the existing Pyomo/JuMP engines. Can also run Excel-based templates.
"Find the minimum-cost design that meets these load constraints" → calls Pyomo solver iteratively
Reads screenshots, CAD images, and Excel charts using image recognition.
"Analyze this kinematic graph and tell me if it meets constraints"

The ingestion pipeline is the foundation of the RAG system. It takes all of optArrow's documents (source code, documentation, solver manuals, Excel templates) and converts them into searchable vector embeddings stored in the vector database. Without this pipeline, the AI has nothing to search.
1. LOAD: Read each document file from disk (Python code, Julia code, Markdown docs, PDFs, Excel files).

2. CHUNK: Split each document into smaller pieces ("chunks") of 300-600 tokens. The splitting strategy depends on the file type — code is split at function boundaries, docs at headings, PDFs at page blocks.
3. TAG: Attach metadata to each chunk (source file, section name, language, component, content hash, version) so we can filter and cite results later.
4. EMBED: Convert each chunk's text into a vector (a list of 1024 numbers) using an embedding model. Similar texts produce similar vectors.
5. STORE: Save the vectors + metadata into the Qdrant vector database for fast similarity search.
Each file type in optArrow needs a different chunking approach to preserve meaning:
Pyomo model definitions, FastAPI routes, utility functions
AST-aware: split at function/class boundaries. Include docstring + signature in every chunk.
Splitting mid-function destroys meaning. A Pyomo constraint block must stay together.
Regex: split at function...end blocks. Keep full function intact.
Julia functions use end delimiters. JuMP constraint blocks must not be split.
Docs site pages, README, API reference
Heading-aware: split at ## headings. Embed heading text into each chunk.
Each heading = one topic. The heading provides essential retrieval context.
Layout-aware (PyMuPDF): extract text blocks, keep math formulations together.
Solver docs contain mathematical notation that must not be split mid-equation.
Extract cell formulas and named ranges as structured text.
Formulas encode business logic that the AI needs to understand.
MATLAB functions end with 'end' or EOF. Must keep complete functions.
Every chunk gets enriched with traceability metadata. This metadata serves two critical purposes (from the architecture specification):
Purpose 1: Filter results during retrieval. For example, if a user asks about Julia code, we can pre-filter to only search chunks where language="julia", making results more precise.
Purpose 2: Cite the exact document version and section in the final answer. This is essential for compliance and trust — the user needs to verify the AI's sources.
Know which file the chunk came from
Filter by document type during retrieval
Detect changes; avoid re-indexing unchanged content
Track when this chunk was last indexed

Per the architecture specification, the ingestion pipeline runs as an async cron job (weekly or nightly) to pick up new documents, code changes, and updated solver manuals. It uses the content_hash to avoid re-processing unchanged files. The schedule is configurable (default: every Monday at 2:00 AM).

An embedding model converts text into a vector (a list of numbers). Similar texts produce similar vectors, which is how we find relevant documents when a user asks a question. We embed both the documents (at ingestion time) and the user's query (at search time), then find the closest matches.
Trained specifically on code; best retrieval quality for mixed Python/Julia/docs corpus
Strong general-purpose model; cheaper per token
Runs entirely locally; no data leaves the machine

Qdrant is a purpose-built vector database that stores embeddings and enables fast similarity search. We chose Qdrant because it is production-ready, Docker-friendly, supports metadata filtering (essential for filtering by doc_type, language, component), and has excellent Python client support.
Qdrant runs as a Docker container alongside the existing optArrow services:

The vector store creates payload indexes on doc_type, language, and component fields. This means when the Research Agent searches for "Julia code about constraint handling," it can pre-filter to only search Julia chunks, dramatically improving precision and speed.

Retrieval is a two-stage process. Stage 1 (fast, approximate) retrieves 20 candidate chunks from the vector database using ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) search. Stage 2 (slow, precise) re-scores those 20 candidates using a cross-encoder reranker and returns only the top 5. This two-stage approach is standard in production RAG systems because it balances speed with quality.

The Iteration Agent drives optimisation loops. This is the critical integration point with the existing optArrow system. It does NOT replace the Pyomo/JuMP engines — it wraps them. When it needs to run an optimisation, it calls the existing /optimize endpoint internally (via HTTP), which routes through the existing Arrow Flight RPC (for Pyomo) or TCP Socket (for JuMP) to the existing solvers.
Calls the existing /optimize endpoint to run Pyomo or JuMP models with specified solver and parameters.
EXISTING: Pyomo via Arrow Flight RPC, JuMP via TCP Socket, all existing solvers
Loads an Excel template, modifies parameter cells, recalculates, and extracts metrics. Runs on isolated copies.
Extracts charts and labels from Excel files. Computes metrics like torque vs. angle compliance.
Retrieves hard rules from the RAG knowledge base and filters out optimisation candidates that violate them.

The Vision Agent will handle image recognition for CAD screenshots, kinematic graphs, and Excel chart analysis. It will use OCR and multimodal LLM capabilities. This is documented here for completeness but is not part of the initial RAG implementation.

The generation layer is where the AI actually produces answers. It takes the retrieved chunks (from the retriever) and the user's question, constructs a carefully designed prompt, and sends it to an LLM (Large Language Model) to generate a natural language response.
The system prompt explicitly instructs the LLM to:
Answer ONLY from the provided context (no hallucination)
Cite sources with [Source: filename, section] format
Say "I don't have enough information" when context is insufficient
Understand optArrow's architecture (Pyomo, JuMP, solvers, Arrow Flight RPC)
Best reasoning for technical Q&A, code explanation, and mathematical formulations
For environments where no data can leave the machine
Both streaming (SSE) and non-streaming responses are supported. Streaming is recommended for the Copilot Chat UI for a responsive user experience.
